title: Vintage photos show what airport security was like before 9/11
snippet:
Airport security in the 1970s.
Duane Howell/Denver Post via Getty Images

Airport security used to be far more relaxed with fewer screenings and restrictions.
People didn't need plane tickets to get through security, and knives were allowed on flights.
The Transportation Security Administration wasn't established until after 9/11.

Before 9/11, airport security was far more relaxed than it is today.
Friends and family could accompany travelers through security without a boarding pass. Knives and blades were allowed in carry-on bags as long as they were smaller than 4 inches. Private companies, not the government-run Transportation Security Administration, handled screenings.
Airport security did evolve over the decades in response to bombings — like the Pan Am bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988 — as well as hijackings and other threats. X-ray machines and metal detectors slowly became familiar features, but the experience was vastly different compared to modern air travel.
In the aftermath of September 11, airport security transformed almost overnight. These vintage photos show how travelers once navigated a system that now seems unrecognizable.

Before 9/11, checked luggage was not subject to universal explosives screening.
The conveyor belt took baggage to the bus docks at New York's East Side Airlines Terminal.
Orlando /Three Lions/Getty Images



X-ray baggage screenings weren't introduced until the 1950s.
Early airport security X-ray. One of the first X- rays ever taken of the interior of a suitcase, using X-ray surveillance at an airport. Two hand guns have been exposed, with a grenade tucked into the shoe at lower left. This late 1950s image was taken at an airport in the United Kingdom. X-ray fluoroscopy was the process, used by a security device manufactured by Pantak. X-ray checks have since become more sophisticated, but are still only as efficient as the guards analysing these X- rays. In this case the grenade could easily be mistaken for a sock in the shoe, and a gun seen from end on is much harder to recognise.No use: BBC, Pearson, Oxford University Press, Springer Nature, Dorling Kindersley, Cambridge University Press & Assessment, New Scientist, Bonnier Publications, John Wiley & Sons, The Lancet, BMJ
Science Photo Library via Reuters Connect



Signs warned passengers from bringing weapons and explosives, but screenings were lax by today's standards.
Airport officials view are introduced to new signage warning passengers of penalties for making false statements regarding hijacking or carrying weapons aboard an aircraft, 1970.
Federal Aviation Administration/PhotoQuest/Getty Images



More stringent security checks at John F. Kennedy Airport in 1970 caught weapons such as guns, daggers, and hand grenades.
Jan. 1, 1970 - When President Nixon called for the death penalty for sky jackers, this pictured may have helped to influence him. It was taken in the Marshall's office in Brooklyn, New York and represents the results of one week's frisking of passengers passing through Kennedy Airport. Automatics, daggers, ammunition, even a hand greanade all were discovered by the stringent security checks at Kennedy in a seven day period. All the guns were later tested by ballistic experts to find if they had been used in recent times. Then the haul was destroyed.
Keystone Press Agency/ZUMA Press Wire



In 1973, the FAA mandated the use of magnetometers and X-ray machines to screen passengers and carry-ons on commercial flights.
DEC 20 1972; A guard watches as passengers and visitors file through one of the "magnetometer" tunnels at Stapleton International Airport. System, begun Tuesday, is to prevent hijackings.
The Denver Post via Getty Images



Full-body scanners wouldn't arrive until 2007.
2/21/1987, DEC 22 1987; Stapleton Airport "Security" United Airline Pilots going thru security early Monday morning.
John Prieto/Denver Post via Getty Images



Many airports had kiosks with life insurance vending machines geared toward nervous flyers.
Passengers could buy travel insurance at the airport.
Don Cravens/Getty Images



Before 9/11, people who weren't flying could obtain gate passes and access the gate area.
An airport security officer checking carry-on luggage in 1980.
Jacques M. Chenet/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images



There were also no restrictions on bringing liquids or gels in carry-on bags back then.
JUL 15 1973, JUL 16 1973, JUL 17 1973; Passengers on "B" concourse at Stapleton International Airport Pvt hand luggage through new machine installed by Unites Airlines.; (Photo By
John Beard/Denver Post via Getty Images



The first security lines at San Francisco International Airport formed in 1973, with an express line for passengers with no carry-ons.
Feb. 20, 1973: The first security lines at San Francisco International Airport, where passengers were searched after years of minimal security at the airport.
Clem Albers/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images



Separate lines for TSA PreCheck and CLEAR didn't exist yet.
Security at Denver International Airport in 1995.
Brooks Kraft/Sygma via Getty Images



There was no TSA at all — private contractors screened passengers until the federal government took over airport security in 2002.
Feb. 20, 1973: Guards used walkie-talkies to communicate and sticks to inspect bags at the first security lines at San Francisco International Airport.
Clem Albers/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images



The computer monitors used for automated explosives detection systems were much clunkier than they are today.
Automated explosives detection systems at John F. Kennedy International Airport.
Willie Anderson/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images



The knives and box cutters that the hijackers used on 9/11 were legal to bring on planes at the time. After that day, flying was never the same.
394718 01: A Surveillance Camera Photographs Two Men Identified By Authorities As Suspected Hijackers Mohammed Atta (R) And Abdulaziz Alomari (C) As They Pass Through Airport Security September 11, 2001 At Portland International Jetport In Maine. Authorities Say The Two Men Took A Commuter Flight To Boston Before Boarding American Airlines Flight 11, Which Was One Of Four Jetliners Hijacked On September 11 And One Of Two Which Were Crashed Into New York City's World Trade Center.
US Navy/Getty Images

title: 2 Stanford professors explained why telling people to 'follow your passion' is a bad idea
snippet:
Burnett and Evans say the pressure to find one all-consuming passion can make career uncertainty worse.
Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

Stanford professors Bill Burnett and Dave Evans argue that "follow your passion" is bad advice.
Most people don't have a single passion so the advice is often confusing, they say.
On the "Prof G Podcast," Burnett also questioned the idea of your college degree setting your life's direction.

"Follow your passion" has become one of the most repeated pieces of career advice. But Bill Burnett and Dave Evans, Stanford professors and the authors of 'Designing Your Life,' think it can send people in the wrong direction.
"It's probably the worst advice you can give somebody," Burnett said during a live recording of the "Prof G Podcast" with Scott Galloway released on Thursday.
The issue, he said, is that many people don't have a single, obvious passion to follow. Citing research by fellow Stanford scholar Bill Damon, Burnett said: "Less than 20% of people have a singular identifiable passion."
For everyone else, the message can be alienating. "Eight out of 10 people go, 'I don't know what you're talking about,'" Burnett said. Others may have "lots of things" that interest them and no clear way to choose between them.
That can turn a supposedly inspiring instruction into a source of self-doubt. Burnett said that advising people to follow their passion can leave most people feeling: "'I don't know what's wrong with me.'"
Later in the conversation, Burnett offered a different way to approach uncertainty: start with curiosity and run small experiments. "Even if you're really at the lowest of low, there's something you're curious about," he said.
The pair call this approach "prototyping." Rather than making a high-stakes, permanent career decision, people can test an interest by speaking with someone in the field, trying a project, or getting firsthand exposure to the work.
This is especially relevant for workers who feel trapped by an existing degree or career path. Burnett called the idea that people must choose the "right" major a "dysfunctional belief," arguing that a college major is "the way you organize college," not "the way you organize your life."
Evans also pushed back on the idea that work must supply both income and meaning, saying that "meaning-making and money-making don't have to be the same."
The goal, he said, is not to discover a fixed answer to the question of purpose. "There is no figuring it out," he said. "There's only getting on with it."

title: AI might take us all down, just not the way you think
snippet:
"Neither company is acting responsibly," Coxon wrote on X.
Imen Ben Youssef / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter.
You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here.

Please read this newsletter before the end of the world.
I don't mean to be dramatic — ok, maybe a little — but there's a lot of AI apocalypse talk these days.
An Anthropic researcher's resignation and warning earlier this week that AI giants are "gambling with our lives" sparked a wider conversation. Mainly: Is AI actually going to kill us all?
The debate quickly broke into the mainstream, with billionaire hedge fund investor Paul Tudor Jones calling AI a "Category 6 hurricane." Even my 71-year-old mom texted me about whether this was "truth or hysteria."
Let's start with the basics: Can AI really wipe us out? And if so, how would it do it?
BI's Thibault Spirlet posed those questions to senior AI researchers. They outlined short-term risks, like AI fueling human attacks, and wider concerns as we cede more control to AI.
Hollywood has also spent decades imagining how it would all go down.
As for the odds of all this happening, that's a mixed bag. One notable mention is Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI," who said there's a 10% chance AI wipes out humanity in a decade. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher, also spoke to BI about why "AI is not loyal to us."
But why not go straight to the source? We decided to ask AI how it would go about destroying humanity. It turns we'll ultimately be the ones to blame.
Not everyone is taking such a somber view.
The internet is poking fun at some of the alarmist language.
AI companies have made a habit of talking out of both sides of their mouths. Warnings about the tech's "threats" also help them market the power of their products and the important role they play.
That doesn't mean there isn't cause for concern. Many in the AI community have acknowledged they can't slow down even if they wanted to. Losing ground to rivals, or China, isn't an option with so much money at stake.
That still doesn't mean we're on the cusp of something terrible. Fear sells. And dramatic, high-stakes storylines pitched to investors reinforce the idea that these companies are on the frontlines of a revolution, and worth the high price tag.
Because if people stop buying the AI hype, that could pose a real problem for a stock market basically built on it. Fitch Ratings already warned an AI bubble bursting would have a wide-reaching impact.
So AI could take us all down, just not how you think.

title: SpaceX has struck a $1 billion a month compute deal with a mystery customer
snippet:
SpaceX is targeting $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year.
Spencer Platt/Getty Images

SpaceX has closed yet another AI compute deal with a mystery customer.
The agreement is worth over $1 billion a month, SpaceX's CFO said on Thursday.
It follows similar deals with Anthropic and Google as Elon Musk's rocket company cashes in on its Colossus data centers.

SpaceX is cashing in on the surging demand for AI compute.
CFO Bret Johnsen told a Goldman Sachs conference on Thursday that SpaceX had clinched another major data center deal worth over $1 billion a month.
"Just earlier this month, we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year," Johnsen said.
Johnsen did not say who the customer was, but added that the deal gave him "even more conviction" that SpaceX would hit its target of $100 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year.
The latest deal adds to agreements SpaceX has struck with Google and Anthropic to rent out capacity in its massive Colossus data centers in Mississippi and Tennessee.
Anthropic agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion a month through to May 2029 as it battled to meet growing demand for its Claude AI model, while the deal Google, which is a major SpaceX shareholder, agreed in June is worth $920 million a month.
Securing compute to run and train the most powerful AI models has become a huge bottleneck for AI companies, with the likes of OpenAI and Meta embarking on multibillion-dollar data center building sprees that have sparked significant public backlash.
The race to gain access to cutting-edge GPUs and data centers has turned into a major revenue opportunity for SpaceX, which acquired a significant amount of unused data center capacity when it merged with Musk's AI startup xAI in February.
Johnsen told investors in the company's Q2 earnings last month that SpaceX had already signed $6.7 billion in cloud services revenue in the first few weeks of the third quarter.
The influx of revenue comes as SpaceX continues to burn eye-watering amounts of money on building new AI infrastructure.
The rocket company spent $16 billion on AI infrastructure in the second quarter of 2026, with executives telling investors to expect similar levels of spending for the rest of the year.
If everything goes to plan, a lot of that infrastructure will end up in space.
Elon Musk has bet that the solution to the public backlash and energy crunch data centers are facing on Earth lies in building a network of AI satellites, and SpaceX is planning to launch its first orbital data centers at the end of next year.

title: Trump snapped at a reporter after a question about his $5,000 promise to voters: 'You're the worst'
snippet:
President Donald Trump speaks to reporters on the tarmac before boarding Air Force One after attending the Republican Midterm Convention.
Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

A reporter asked Trump why he needed to give voters $5,000 if his economic policies were working.
It didn't go well.
He blamed Biden, and leaned forward and glared at her when she tried a follow-up question.

A reporter asked President Donald Trump why he needed to incentivize voters with a $5,000 check if his economic policies were working, and it seemed to strike a nerve.
On Wednesday, Trump told the Republican Party's midterm convention that every US citizen would receive a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November's midterms.
The proposal could cost upward of $1.3 trillion if every US citizen received the payment, though Vice President JD Vance later said wealthy people would be excluded. Joe Lonsdale, the cofounder of Palantir, was among the critics of the pledge and said the payment would be akin to a "bribe."
When a reporter questioned Trump about the proposal on the airport tarmac in Dallas on Thursday night, the president appeared to snap.
After noting that the US has $40 trillion in debt, the reporter asked: "If your economic policies are working, why do you need an incentive for people to turn out and vote?"
Trump responded: "I didn't do it for turning out the vote. I'm doing it as a reward for people having to put up with five years, and four years, of a horrible, horrible situation caused by Biden."
He repeated the point, calling the promised dividend "almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden's policies."

Q: On the checks, we have $40 trillion in debt. If your economic policies are working, why do you need an incentive for people to turn out to vote?
TRUMP: I'm doing it as a reward for people having to put up for five years and four years of a horrible situation caused by Biden… pic.twitter.com/Iq4LpS1pNt
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) September 11, 2026
 
As the reporter began a follow-up question, Trump said "not you," while pointing to another journalist.
The reporter continued: "You also offered checks during… tariff refunds checks, and that didn't happen, Mr. President."
This was a reference to Trump's November 2025 pledge to send $2,000 tariff-rebate checks, which have not been paid out. He also floated "DOGE dividends" in early 2025, which would have provided Americans with a one-time check of up to $5,000. They also never materialized.
Trump interrupted with another "not you," then leaned toward her, glared, and repeated it for a third time. "Your network and you, you're the worst," he said.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
